titleEn: Laws of Hammurabi — §185–194: adopted children, foster-parents and the wet-nurse (xxxii 31 – xxxiii 40)
part: Laws §185–194 · adoption, foster-children & the wet-nurse (Col. xxxii 31 – xxxiii 40)
about: Ten laws on children taken in and brought up by someone other than their parents. A man who takes a newborn as his son and raises him cannot be made to give him back (§185); but if the child, when taken, keeps looking for his father and mother, he goes back to his father’s house (§186). The sons of two classes of people, a NER.SE.GA and a woman of the zikrum class, cannot be claimed back (§187). A craftsman who takes a foster-son and teaches him his craft keeps him; if he has not taught him, the boy goes back to his father’s house (§188–189). A man who took a child as his son and raised him but did not count him among his sons sends him back to his father’s house (§190). If he has set up a household and later has sons of his own and sets his face to cast the adopted son out, the boy shall not go away empty-handed: the father who raised him gives him one third of an heir’s share from his goods, but nothing from field, orchard or house (§191). The sons of a NER.SE.GA or of a zikrum-woman who say to the foster-father and foster-mother “You are not my father, you are not my mother” have their tongue cut off (§192); if they find out their father’s house, turn away from the foster-parents and go to it, their eye is plucked out (§193). The last law is the wet-nurse: if a man gives his son to a wet-nurse and the child dies in her care, and she then takes another child without his father and mother knowing, they convict her and cut off her breast (§194). The punishments are exactly as the stele states them. Two or three words (NER.SE.GA, the zikrum class, iḫīaṭ, iṣīrma) cannot be read with certainty; the notes say so each time.

sentences.l: If a-man a-young-child in-his-waters as sonship has-taken-and has-raised-him,
sentences.i: If a man has taken a young child as his son while he was still in his waters (that is, a newborn?) and has raised him,
sentences.n: The first of ten laws on adoption and foster-children; like every law of the code it is one “if” sentence, cut here at its verbs. šumma awīlum is “if a man”. ṣeḫram is “a young child” (ṣeḫrum with the accusative -am), the object. ina mêšu is “in his waters”: mû “water”, plural mê, with -šu “his”; I take it as the child’s birth-waters, so “a newborn”, but that is UNCERTAIN — no other use of the phrase turns up in these parts. ana mārūtim is “as sonship, as a son”: mārūtum, the abstract in -ūtum of mārum “son”, in the genitive after ana; this is the adoption formula. ilqēma is “he took, and”: ilqi, the preterite of leqûm, plus -ma (spelled il-qi₂-ma, the KI sign read qi₂). urtabbišu is “he has raised him”: the perfect (the infixed -ta-) of the D-stem of rabûm “to be great”, which means “to bring up”: urabbi, “he raises”, becomes urtabbi, with -šu “him”.

sentences.l: that foster-child not shall-be-claimed.
sentences.i: No claim shall be made on that foster-child.
sentences.n: The apodosis, and a short one. tarbītum is “what is brought up, the foster-child”, a noun built on the same D-stem as urtabbišu above. It is feminine, so “that” is šī, not šū. ul ibbaqqar is “no claim shall be made”: the N-stem (the passive) present of baqārum “to claim”, as in §112–126 and earlier. Harper prints ib-ba-ag-gar, the AK sign read ag; I write aq, q as everywhere. The law does not name who might claim the child; the next law shows it is the birth-parents.

sentences.l: If a-man a-young-child as sonship has-taken,
sentences.i: If a man has taken a young child as his son,
sentences.n: The same opening as §185, but the verb is a bare ilqi “he took” (il-qi₂, no -ma): the sentence is not finished, a second clause follows in the next unit. On the stele il-qi₂ stands on a second tier below the end of stele line 41 (Harper’s {b}).

sentences.l: when he-took-him, his-father and his-mother he-seeks(?),
sentences.i: when he took him, he keeps looking for (?) his father and his mother,
sentences.n: A clause with inūma “when”, whose verb is therefore in the subjunctive: ilqûšu is ilqi + the subjunctive -u (the two vowels contract to û) + -šu “him”, “when he took him”. abašu and ummašu are “his father” and “his mother”, in the accusative (abam, ummam + šu): they are the objects of the last verb. iḫīaṭ (i-ḫi-a-aṭ) I read as a present of ḫiāṭum “to look out for, to seek”: UNCERTAIN, I know the verb only as a 1904-era gloss and the sense “seek out” is what the next lines call for. Nor does the clause say who the subject is; I take it to be the child, who longs for his birth-parents, but the man is also possible grammatically.

sentences.l: that foster-child to the-house of-his-father shall-return.
sentences.i: That foster-child shall go back to his father’s house.
sentences.n: ana bīt abišu is “to the house of his father”: bīt “house of” is the bare sign É (the construct form, no ending written), abišu “of his father” is in the genitive. itâr is “he/she shall return”, the present of târum; the same formula as bītum ana bēlīšu itâr “the house returns to its owner” in §66–78. Here “his father” is the child’s birth-father.

sentences.l: The-son of-NER.SE.GA (?), (one) standing-of the-palace, and the-son of-a-woman, a-zikrum (?),
sentences.i: The son of a NER.SE.GA (?), one who stands in the palace’s service, and the son of a woman of the zikrum class (?),
sentences.n: A law with no “if”: it opens with the persons it is about, and the next unit says what is true of them. mār is “son of” (DUMU); as in §188 mār X can also mean a member of the group X. NER.SE.GA is a Sumerogram of three signs, KIŠ read ner (Harper’s sign list no. 170), the tall chevron-stack sign (his no. 76, se) and GA; it is the same group on the plate at §192 and §193 (XXXII 96, XXXIII 10). I cannot read it and leave it so — a class or title of person, UNCERTAIN. mūzaz ekallim is “one who stands of the palace”: mūzaz is a participle of izuzzum “to stand” (compare izzazzu “he stands (in service)”), ekallim “of the palace” (the two signs É and GAL, no ending written), so “a palace attendant”; whether it names the same man as NER.SE.GA or is a second description I cannot tell. u mār zinništim zikrum is “and the son of a woman, a zikrum”: zinništim (the sign SAL alone), then zi-ik-ru-um, the class-name of §178–180, UNCERTAIN. On the plate zi is the barred wedge with a stack of chevrons (Harper’s no. 41); the tall chevron sign in NER.SE.GA is a different, upright one (no. 76), which I key as SHE (ŠE), the nearest house key — UNCERTAIN.

sentences.l: not shall-be-claimed.
sentences.i: No claim shall be made on them.
sentences.n: The apodosis of §187, the same formula as §185. The verb is singular for two subjects, as often in the code.

sentences.l: If a-son of-the-craftsmen a-son for-rearing has-taken-and,
sentences.i: If a craftsman (lit. a son of the craftsmen) has taken a son as a foster-child and
sentences.n: mār ummiānim is “a son of a craftsman”, that is, a member of the craftsman class (compare mārū ugārim “the sons of the irrigated land” = the farmers): ummiānim is UM.MI.A, three signs with no ending written; Harper prints ummânim, and his own list of signs gives the same group as mâr-ummâni. The second mâram “a son” is DUMU alone. ana tarbītim is “for rearing, as a foster-child”: tarbītum is here an ordinary noun in the genitive after ana, the purpose of the taking.

sentences.l: the-work of-his-hands he-has-taught-him, not shall-be-claimed.
sentences.i: and has taught him the work of his hands, no claim shall be made.
sentences.n: šipir qātīšu is “the work of his hands”, that is, his craft: šipir is the construct of šiprum “work”, qātīšu “his hands” (qātum + -šu). Harper prints ši-bi-ir ga-ti-šu; the BI sign is also read pi₂ and GA is also read qa₂, so the same signs give šipir qātīšu. uštāḫissu is the perfect of the Š-stem of aḫāzum “to take hold”: ušta-ḫiz “he has made (him) take hold”, with -šu “him”, whose š after the z becomes ss and is written with the sign ZU (compare bīssu, mussa). So “he has taught him”, from “made him grasp”; the sense follows from the Š-stem, compare ušaḫḫazūšu “they shall have him take (a wife)”. The principal clause is again ul ibbaqqar (Harper prints ib-ba-gar, one g).

sentences.l: If the-work of-his-hands not he-has-taught-him,
sentences.i: If he has not taught him the work of his hands,
sentences.n: The opposite case to §188. lā is “not” in an “if” clause (as lā ītamar “he did not see” earlier); uštāḫissu is the same verb as above. On the stele šum-ma and ši-bi-ir stand on one tier and ga-ti-šu is on a second tier below (Harper’s {b}).

sentences.l: that foster-child to the-house of-his-father shall-return.
sentences.i: That foster-child shall go back to his father’s house.
sentences.n: As §186: the foster-child goes back to his birth-father’s house when the craft has not been taught.

sentences.l: If a-man a-young-child whom as-his-sonship he-took-him-and raised-him,
sentences.i: If a man has taken a young child as his son and raised him,
sentences.n: A different construction from §185: the young child is introduced first and the rest hangs on him as a relative clause. ša opens it (“whom”), and the verbs of a ša-clause end in the subjunctive -u, here in ilqûšuma “he took him, and” (ilqi + -u + -šu “him” + -ma) and urabbûšu “he raised him” (urabbi + -u + -šu, the BU sign standing for the contracted bû). The “him” inside the clause points back at the child, which English does not need; the English line leaves the relative out.

sentences.l: with his-sons not he-has-counted-him,
sentences.i: and has not counted him among his sons,
sentences.n: itti mārīšu is “with his sons” (DUMU{meš} + -šu); imtanûšu is “he has counted him”, the perfect of manûm “to count” with -šu “him”, in the subjunctive (-nû). lā imtanûšu is “he has not counted him”, in the sense of not reckoning him among his heirs; it is the third verb of the relative clause, with no -ma between them.

sentences.l: that foster-child to-the-house of-his-father shall-return.
sentences.i: That foster-child shall go back to his father’s house.

sentences.l: If a-man a-young-child whom as-his-sonship he-took-him-and raised-him,
sentences.i: If a man has taken a young child as his son and raised him,
sentences.n: The same protasis as §190. At XXXII 79 the stele has an extra U sign, u-ra-ab-bu-u-šu, for the same word urabbûšu.

sentences.l: his-house he-made, afterwards sons he-has-acquired-and,
sentences.i: has set up a house of his own, and afterwards has acquired sons, and
sentences.n: bīssu ipuš is “he made his house” (epēšum “to make”, ipuš the preterite): to set up a household of one’s own. bīssu is “his house”: the bīt sign É with ZU for -ssu (t + š becomes ss, as in bīssa, mussa); Harper prints bí-zu. warka is “afterwards” (as in §170–177); mārī is “sons”, accusative plural (DUMU{meš}); irtašima is irtaši “he has acquired” (the perfect of rašûm) + -ma.

sentences.l: to the-foster-child to-cast-out face he-has-set,
sentences.i: and has set his face to cast out the foster-child,
sentences.n: panam ištakan is “he has set (his) face”, a phrase for resolving to do something, as in §170–177, “set her face to go out”. ana tarbītim nasāḫim is “to cast out the foster-child”: ana with the object tarbītim, then the infinitive nasāḫim, “for the casting out of the foster-child”; for nasāḫum “to cast out, disinherit” see §153–169.

sentences.l: that son empty-handed (?) not shall-go.
sentences.i: that son shall not go away empty-handed (?).
sentences.n: mārum šū is “that son”. Harper prints tal-ku-zu, which I cannot make into a word; the signs are RI (the sign Harper reads tal as well as ri), KU (qu₂) and ZU, and read ri-qu₂-zu they give rīqūssu, “his emptiness”, from rēqum “empty”, as an adverb “empty-handed”: with the ZU = -ssu of bīssu above. UNCERTAIN; it arrived as a recognition rather than from the sign values alone, and the context (the next unit says what he does get) supports it. ul ittallak is “he shall not go”, the present of alākum.

sentences.l: the-father who-raised-him from his-property one-third-of his-heirship shall-give-him-and he-shall-go.
sentences.i: The father who raised him shall give him from his property one third of his heir’s share, and he shall go away.
sentences.n: abum murabbīšu is “the father, his rearer”: murabbīšu is the participle of the D-stem of rabûm (the prefix mu- makes it “one who raises”) with -šu “him”. ina makkūršu is “from his property”: makkūršu, the Sumerogram Harper reads ŠA.GA (two signs) + šu. šalšat ablūtišu is “one third of his heir’s share”, as at §178–184 (IGI.3.GAL, three signs); ablūtišu is ablūtum “sonship, the status of an heir” + -šu. inaddiššumma is “he shall give him, and” (inaddin + -šum “to him” + -ma, spelled with iš-šum, the TAG sign read šum). ittalak is “he goes”, here an order: “he shall go away”.

sentences.l: from field, orchard and house not he-shall-give-him.
sentences.i: From the field, the orchard and the house he shall not give him anything.
sentences.n: ina eqlim kirîm u bītim is “from the field, the orchard and the house”: eqlim is the Sumerogram A.ŠÀ with the complement lim, kirîm the wood-sign and the SAR sign read KIRI₆ (as in §26–41), bītim the bare sign É. ul inaddiššum is “he shall not give him”: the verb is the same inaddiššum as above (said short, the u before -šum), written across two stele lines, i-na-ad-di- at the end of XXXII 94 and iš-šum on XXXII 95. “Anything” is not written and is added in English.

sentences.l: If the-son of-NER.SE.GA or the-son of-a-woman, a-zikrum (?),
sentences.i: If the son of a NER.SE.GA (?) or the son of a woman of the zikrum class (?),
sentences.n: The same two persons as §187, now in an “if” clause: ù lū (u lu) is “or else”, as at §178–184. The unit runs across Harper’s column break (the plate has the heading COLUMN XXXIII between XXXII 96 and XXXIII 1), and the line XXXIII 1 stands on two tiers. NER.SE.GA and the zikrum class are UNCERTAIN, as in §187.

sentences.l: to the-father who-raised-him and to-the-mother who-raised-him
sentences.i: to the father who raised him and the mother who raised him
sentences.n: ana abim is “to the father”; murabbīšu is “his rearer”, the participle of the D-stem of rabûm + -šu, as in §191; the feminine is murabbītīšu, “his female rearer”, spelled out with the ti sign (murabbītum + -šu).

sentences.l: not my-father you, not my-mother you he-has-said,
sentences.i: has said, “You are not my father; you are not my mother,”
sentences.n: A quotation of two nominal sentences, each “not X you”: ul abī atta is “you are not my father” (abī “my father”, atta “you”, masculine) and ul ummī atti “you are not my mother” (atti is the feminine “you”). The verb is the last word: iqtabi “he has said”, the perfect of qabûm, as at §170–177. Both lines stand on two tiers on the stele.

sentences.l: his-tongue they-shall-cut-off.
sentences.i: they shall cut off his tongue.
sentences.n: The sentence is exactly as the stele has it; nothing is softened. lišānšu is “his tongue”: the EME sign (a KA sign with ME inside, Harper’s list no. 13, lišânu) + -šu. inakkisū is “they shall cut off”: the present plural of nakāsum “to cut”, with no named subject, “they” being those who carry out the sentence. The last two sounds, s and the plural ending -ū, are written with the one sign su (i-na-ak-ki-su; Harper prints su, not šu).

sentences.l: If the-son of-NER.SE.GA or the-son of-a-woman, a-zikrum, his-father’s-house has-identified (?) and,
sentences.i: If the son of a NER.SE.GA (?) or the son of a woman of the zikrum class (?) has identified (?) his father’s house, and
sentences.n: The same two persons as §192. uwaddīma (u-wi-id-di-ma) is uwaddi + -ma: I read it as the D-stem of edûm “to know” (compare mūdi “knower of”), “to make known, to point out”, so “he has identified, found out” his father’s house: UNCERTAIN. bīt abišu is again the bare sign É + “of his father”.

sentences.l: the-father who-raised-him and the-mother who-raised-him has-turned-from (?) and,
sentences.i: has turned away from (?) the father who raised him and the mother who raised him, and
sentences.n: abam and ummam are “the father” and “the mother” in the accusative, the objects of iṣīrma; murabbīšu “his rearer”, murabbīssu “his female rearer”: the feminine murabbītum + -šu, with t + š written ss by the ZU sign (compare the spelled-out murabbītīšu in §192). iṣīrma (i-ṣi-ir-ma) is a verb I cannot place: i-ṣīr + -ma; I read it as “has turned away from, has been hostile to”, from a root ṣiārum that I cannot confirm: UNCERTAIN, and the sense is taken from the sequence “finds out his father’s house, turns from the foster-parents, goes to the house”.

sentences.l: to the-house of-his-father he-has-gone,
sentences.i: and has gone to his father’s house,
sentences.n: ittalak is “he has gone”, the perfect of alākum, the last verb of the long “if” clause.

sentences.l: his-eye they-shall-pluck-out.
sentences.i: they shall pluck out his eye.
sentences.n: Again exactly as the stele has it. īnšu is “his eye” (īnum + -šu); inassaḫū is “they shall pluck out”, the present plural of nasāḫum “to pull out” (house rendering for “uproot”), with the double s written with the ZA sign, i-na-za-ḫu (compare a-na-za-aḫ in §153–169), and the plural ending -ū fused into the ḫu sign. No subject is named, as in §192.

sentences.l: If a-man his-son to a-wet-nurse he-gave-and,
sentences.i: If a man has given his son to a wet-nurse and
sentences.n: mārašu is “his son” (DUMU + šu, accusative); ana mušēniqtim is “to a wet-nurse”: mušēniqtum is the Š-participle of the verb enēqum “to suck”, the one who makes (a child) suck. It is built from the grammar (mu- + the Š-stem sign še + ni-iq + the feminine -t-), so the sense “wet-nurse” rests on the form and on the law that follows, not on a word listed in these parts. iddinma is “he gave, and”: iddin the preterite of nadānum + -ma.

sentences.l: that son in-the-hand of-the-wet-nurse has-died,
sentences.i: and that son has died in the wet-nurse’s care (lit. in the hand of the wet-nurse),
sentences.n: ina qāt mušēniqtim is “in the hand of the wet-nurse”: qāt is the bare construct of qātum “hand”; here the Akkadian means “in her keeping”, and the English says it both ways. imtūt is “he has died”, the perfect of mâtum, as in the earlier laws.

sentences.l: the-wet-nurse without his-father and his-mother another-son has-bound,
sentences.i: the wet-nurse has taken on (lit. bound herself to) another son without his father and mother (knowing),
sentences.n: mušēniqtum is the subject, in the nominative. balum abišu u ummišu is “without his father and his mother” (balum “without” + genitives), and “his” is the dead child’s father and mother. mārām šaniamma is “another son” (accusative; šaniam “another”, -ma “indeed”). irtakas is “he/she has bound”: the perfect of rakāsum “to bind” (not the D-stem met earlier); to “bind oneself to” a child is to take it on, so “taken on”. That is the sense I infer from the context: UNCERTAIN, and “(knowing)” is added in English, since balum “without” covers “without their knowledge or agreement”.

sentences.l: they-shall-convict-her-and,
sentences.i: they shall convict her, and
sentences.n: ukannūšima is ukannūši + -ma: the D-stem of kânum “to be firm”, which means “to prove (a case) against, to convict”, plural (impersonal “they”), with -ši “her” and -ma “and”. Compare ukannūšuma “they shall convict him, and” earlier in the code. The next clause gives the reason, and the penalty follows after it.

sentences.l: because without his-father and his-mother another son she-bound,
sentences.i: because she bound another son without his father and mother (knowing),
sentences.n: aššum is “because”, and the verb of its clause is in the subjunctive: irkusu (ir-ku-šu), irkus + -u. Harper prints the last sign as šu; I read it as su here, the subjunctive of rakāsum, but the sign is the same as in the šu of -šu. The rest repeats the charge of the last unit.

sentences.l: her-breast they-shall-cut-off.
sentences.i: they shall cut off her breast.
sentences.n: The penalty, as the stele states it, unsoftened. tulêša is “her breast”: tulê (the plural form of tulûm, “breasts”, as body-words often are; I give the singular since the Akkadian often means one) + ša “her”. It is written with a single Sumerogram (Harper’s list no. 105, tulû, three connected parts, which I take for the sign UBUR, a tentative identification) and the syllable ša. inakkisū as in §192.
